meta.title: Danish A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Danish → English (see the Danish, recall the meaning) and English → Danish (see an English meaning, recall the Danish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words of Danish for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to communicate in simple and routine tasks requiring a simple and direct exchange of information on familiar and routine matters, and to describe in simple terms aspects of their background, immediate environment and matters in areas of immediate need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Danish has examinations at these levels — Prøve i Dansk 1, 2 and 3 and Studieprøven — but none was found to publish a word list, so this deck is not an examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 287 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the seasons and dates, more numbers, the land and nature, the weather, animals, clothes, the home and the kitchen, food and cooking, work and jobs, school, travel and transport, the town, health, feelings, free time, the everyday verbs of these, describing things and people, time words, and the words that join one clause to the next — and the other 463 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Danish, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The 361 nouns are printed with their article — en or et — because the article is the gender, which decides the noun's definite ending, the adjective's ending and the pronoun that stands for it, and they show their definite singular and their plural (bilen, biler); the 193 verbs show their present, their past and their perfect with its auxiliary (spiser, spiste, har spist; går, gik, er gået), since Danish chooses between have and være by the verb, and behind the All forms fold their imperative, -s forms and participles. Real example sentences come with 737 of the 750 words, three apiece for 700 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.

We have not immortal souls, we shall never live again; like the green seaweed when once it has been cut off, we can never flourish more. Human beings, on the contrary, have souls which live forever, even after the body has been turned to dust. They rise up through the clear, pure air, beyond the glittering stars.
